Compare Built-In Group Testing Designs

Source: R/compare_designs.R
compare_all_designs.Rd

Generate several built-in pooling designs and summarize their structural properties in a common comparison object. The current implementation compares the package constructors for P-BEST, Tapestry, HYPER, and the package-specific experimental parity-augmented hyper_ec_matrix() extension.

Usage

compare_all_designs(n = 256, prevalence = 0.01, alpha = 0.2)

Arguments

n

Integer scalar giving the target number of individuals. This is the intended column dimension \(N\) for the Tapestry, HYPER, and experimental HYPER-EC comparison branches. The default is 256.

prevalence

Numeric scalar giving the assumed common prevalence \(p_i = p\) used to define the approximate expected number of positives \(k = \max\{1, \lfloor Np \rfloor\}\) for design constructors that require an input sparsity level. It must lie in \((0,1)\); the default is 0.01.

alpha

Numeric scalar giving the parity-overhead factor for the package-specific experimental hyper_ec_matrix() branch. The default is 0.20. In that branch the number of added parity pools is driven by \(\alpha\).

Value

A named list with five components:

pbest

A list with components matrix and metrics for the P-BEST branch.

tapestry

A list with components matrix and metrics for the Tapestry branch.

hyper

A list with components matrix and metrics for the HYPER branch.

hyper_ec

A list with components matrix and metrics for the experimental parity-augmented HYPER-EC branch.

comparison_table

A data frame with one row per design and columns Design, Samples_n, Pools_m, Efficiency_m_n, Lambda_max, and Error_Correction.

Each metrics component is itself a named list. For successful design generation it contains summary statistics such as the achieved number of individuals \(N\), the number of pools \(J\), the ratio \(J/N\), the maximum column sum \(\max_i |\mathcal{J}_i|\), and row-size summaries based on \(n_j = |\mathcal{P}_j|\). If a branch fails, its metrics entry contains a design label and a failure note. The Error_Correction field is a package-specific comparison label for this helper; it is not a formal paper-backed guarantee.

Details

Let \(\mathbf{M} \in \{0,1\}^{J \times N}\) denote a pooling matrix, where \(N\) is the number of individuals and \(J\) is the number of pools. This function builds one design object for each supported branch and reports a common set of structural summaries. For every successfully generated design, the comparison metrics are derived from $$n_j = |\mathcal{P}_j| = \sum_{i=1}^N M_{ji}$$ and $$w_i = |\mathcal{J}_i| = \sum_{j=1}^J M_{ji}.$$ The reported efficiency ratio is $$\frac{J}{N},$$ which is stored in the output as Efficiency_m_n. The reported Lambda_max is a display label for the maximum number of pools containing any single individual, $$\lambda_{\max} = \max_{1 \le i \le N} |\mathcal{J}_i| = \max_i w_i.$$ The row-size summaries are the empirical mean and standard deviation of \(n_j\).

The comparison procedure uses the following package-specific constructor choices. For Tapestry and the experimental HYPER-EC branch, the expected number of positives is approximated by $$k = \max\left\{1, \left\lfloor N p \right\rfloor\right\}.$$ For HYPER, the baseline number of pools is set heuristically to $$J_{\mathrm{base}} = \max\left\{\left\lceil 4 k \log(N) \right\rceil, \left\lceil 0.15 N \right\rceil\right\},$$ followed by an adjustment to the nearest even integer so that the q = 2 constructor call is admissible. The P-BEST branch always uses the package's fixed standard constructor call pp_matrix(q = 8, d = 3, nl = 6, N = 384), so its achieved column dimension is not forced to equal the input n. The experimental HYPER-EC branch uses hyper_ec_matrix(n = n, k = k, m_base = m_hyper, q = 2, alpha = alpha) and should be interpreted as a package-specific extension rather than the Hong et al. HYPER paper design.

References

Shental, N., Levy, S., Wuvshet, V., et al. (2020). Efficient high-throughput SARS-CoV-2 testing to detect asymptomatic carriers. Science Advances, 6(37), eabc5961.

Ghosh, S., Agarwal, R., Rehan, M. A., et al. (2021). Tapestry: A single-round smart pooling technique for COVID-19 testing. Nature Communications, 12, Article 2995.

Hong, F. S., Shah, N., Briggs, A., et al. (2022). HYPER group testing for SARS-CoV-2: A flexible, easy-to-implement, and highly efficient method. Nature Communications, 13, Article 3626.

Aldridge, M., Johnson, O., & Scarlett, J. (2019). Group testing: An information theory perspective. Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, 15(3-4), 196-392.

See also

pp_matrix, tapestry_matrix, hyper_matrix, hyper_ec_matrix, compare_designs

comparison <- compare_all_designs(n = 128, prevalence = 0.01, alpha = 0.20)
